artboards.title: As they stand today — two screens, one shelf
Proposed — the Pricing console, a thin line open
Proposed — not moving: a price, a verdict, and who has taken it before
Proposed — nothing to fix, nothing to judge, and a failure

annotations.text:
THE JOB OF THIS SCREEN

Margin and Clearance were the same question asked twice about one shelf, and neither could see the other's half.

A line you stock is in exactly one of three states: selling and keeping enough, SELLING BUT THIN, or NOT SELLING AT ALL. The first needs nothing from you. The second two are both price decisions -- lift it, or cut it and find somebody who has bought it before -- so they are one queue, ranked by what a fix is worth. That is the whole idea.

You settled four things and everything here follows from them.

1. ONE QUEUE, RANKED BY MONEY. Not two panels and not two groups. The ranking is the answer to "what do I do first", and it can only answer that if both kinds of problem are in it.

2. THE NAME IS "PRICING". Both halves are a price decision. "Your margin" and "Clearance" stay as search keywords, so the word already in somebody's head still finds the door -- the same thing Debtors and Creditors did with their old names.

3. THE OFFER LIVES INSIDE THE OPEN LINE. An offer is about ONE line, so it is written on that line, beside the price it is offering. The old "Who has taken these before" panel -- a whole second console below the list -- is gone.

4. THE ACCENT IS ONE BUTTON, INSIDE THE ONE OPEN ROW. Today Margin puts an oxide "Charge 58,600" on EVERY row. Fourteen accents is no accent.

Everything is drawn from index.html's own values: the 23-colour palette, the 11/12/13/14 ramp, Inter + Archivo Black + IBM Plex Mono, and the .ow-* console components already shipping on Today, Debtors, Chase debts, Follow-ups, Consignment and Creditors. No new colour, no new weight, no new type size, no fourteenth button family.

WHAT IS WRONG WITH THEM AS THEY STAND, BOTH SCREENS >

1. THE SHELF IS SPLIT DOWN THE MIDDLE AND NEITHER HALF SAYS SO. Margin reads what SOLD; Clearance reads what did NOT. Neither names the other, so no screen in the app can tell you what your shelf as a whole is doing. "5,410,000 sitting dead" and "2,580,000 a month left on the table" are the same shop's money, and you have to hold them in your head.

2. FOURTEEN OXIDE BUTTONS ON THE MARGIN SCREEN. One "Charge X" per row, and the accent is meant to appear once per screen -- it is the one thing to do next. Fourteen of them is a screen with no next thing on it.

3. A 640-CHARACTER PARAGRAPH AND A 620-CHARACTER ONE, unmeasured, sitting open above the money. On a 1660px screen those run past 180 characters a line. The console header is a name, one line, a hairline; the long version goes behind the "i". Six screens already do this. These two are what is left.

4. A FORM PANEL EACH, FOR ONE NUMBER. "The share you mean to keep" and "When a line counts as dead" are 18/20-padded panels with an icon, a title, a subtitle and a single field -- about 120px apiece, above the list, on every visit, to hold a setting you change twice a year.

5. TWO STRIPS THAT LOOK IDENTICAL AND MEAN DIFFERENT THINGS. Both are .sum-strip, both four cells, both 21px mono. One counts lines under target; the other counts shillings on a shelf. Same shape, different units, different screens -- the shape teaches you nothing.

6. A LIVE NUMBER INPUT ON EVERY CLEARANCE ROW. Twenty-two open fields when one line is being decided, each with a placeholder that CLIPS -- "a price you would take" is cut mid-word, which is fault one of the truncation rule: an <input> cannot ellipsis.

7. THE OFFERS ARE A SECOND CONSOLE BELOW THE FIRST. Every marked line gathered into one message per buyer, at the bottom of the page, away from the price that produced it. To change a figure you scroll up, retype, scroll down and re-read the message.

8. THE ROWS ARE CARDS, NOT ROWS. 12px radius, 13/15 padding, a coloured left rail on stale and marked -- roughly 100px of height per line where the console's row is 44px and opens in place. Eight lines fill a desktop screen.

9. COLOUR THAT MARKS EVERYTHING. The left rail is on every stale row and every marked row, so on a working shelf it is on most of them.

10. OFF-SYSTEM VALUES THROUGHOUT -- sizes 10.5, 11.5, 12.5, 13.5; radius 12 and 9 where the system is 4/6/8; a drop shadow where depth in this app is hairlines; 700 weight where the ramp says 600.

11. NEITHER SCREEN CAN SAY WHAT IT DID NOT READ, TOGETHER. Margin accounts for itself beautifully -- 112 read, 14 thin, 98 fine, 58 uncosted. Clearance does not account for itself at all. And the 58 uncosted lines are exactly the ones neither screen can judge.

THE PROPOSAL -- what changed, and why

ONE STRIP, FOUR QUESTIONS, THE WHOLE SHELF. What you are holding; what is standing still; what share you kept on what moved; what the thin lines cost you in a month. Two of those four are the two halves of the queue below, so the strip and the list can never disagree. "On the shelf" is ink, not a state colour -- stock you hold is a fact, and colouring it would make an ordinary Tuesday look like an alarm.

THE HARD PART, SOLVED IN THE OPEN: TWO KINDS OF MONEY ON ONE LIST. A thin line's figure is income PER MONTH and it repeats. A dead line's is cash locked in the shelf and it comes back ONCE. They are not the same money and must never be summed -- so nothing on this screen ever adds them, every row's basis line says which it is ("a month, if you lift it" / "locked up, once"), and the ranking is done on one stated clock: what a fix is worth OVER A YEAR. A thin line's month counted twelve times, dead stock's cash once. That is why +529,000 a month outranks 1,950,000 sitting on a shelf, and the rail says so in those words so it can be argued with rather than trusted.

THE ROW IS 44px AND CARRIES THE REASON IT IS WHERE IT IS. Name and how it sells, then the reason -- "Keeping 11.2% of 30%", "Quiet 214 days", "Never sold" -- then the basis, then the figure. The reason column never truncates; the name gives way, because a name may be cut and a reason may not. Colour appears only where it means something: crimson on a line genuinely far under, amber on one close, plain grey on stock nobody has ever bought.

THE OPEN LINE IS THE WHOLE DECISION. For a thin line: the sentence in words, then the arithmetic laid out so it can be CHECKED rather than trusted -- cost, what you charge, what keeps target, what the last thirty days would have returned -- then the stale-fixed finding in amber where it applies, then one oxide button. For a dead line: the price you would take, the verdict on that price before the tap, and the buyers who have actually bought it, each with the offer written.

THE TWO SETTINGS ARE IN THE RAIL, beside the sentence that says what each means. Roughly 240px of form panel above the money became two 30px fields you will touch twice a year.

THE ACCOUNT SURVIVES AND NOW COVERS BOTH HALVES. 412 lines read; 14 thin; 22 not moving; 318 fine; 58 with no cost on file and therefore judged by nothing. Margin already did this and it is the best thing on either screen -- it is the only device that lets a reader trust a list for what it does NOT say.

HEIGHT: the paragraph and the form panel came to roughly 300px before the money on each screen. Eight lines and the account are now on the first screen, and there is one screen instead of two.

WHAT I HAVE NOT DECIDED FOR YOU

1. THE RANKING CLOCK. Twelve months for a thin line's month, once for dead stock's cash. That is the honest way to put two kinds of money in one order, and it is stated on screen so it can be argued with. If you would rather dead stock always led -- cash in the drawer beats income on paper when you are short -- it is one comparator, and the sentence in the rail changes with it.

2. THE THIRD STATE IS MISSING FROM THE QUEUE. A line that is BOTH thin AND not moving cannot happen today, because a dead line has no sales to be thin on. But a line selling slowly and thinly is real, and neither screen has ever named it. I have not invented a state for it; say the word and it becomes a third segment.

3. "60 DAYS" AND "30%" ARE STILL TWO NUMBERS YOU SET. I have not merged them or hidden them, only moved them beside the sentence that says what they mean.

4. WHAT I HAVE NOT TOUCHED: the lift arithmetic itself, setLineMarginRule's both-sides write, the offer message text, the clearance stamp, and the CSV. The badge is worth one decision though -- today the rail carries TWO badges, 14 and 22. One screen should carry one number, and I have drawn 36. If you would rather it counted only the thin lines, or only the dead ones, that is a line of code and a real choice about what the rail is for.

5. THE OLD NAMES stay as search keywords: margin, markup, kept, clearance, dead stock, slow, discount, unsold, sitting, offload.

THE OTHER HALF OF THE SAME QUEUE >

Segment on "Not moving", and two lines open at once so the two verdicts can be compared. In the app one line is open at a time.

THE FILTER IS VISIBLE IN THREE PLACES -- the segment, an amber chip with its own X, and a note under the list saying what is hidden and what it is worth. And the strip does NOT move with the filter, which the note says out loud: a position that shrinks because somebody left a filter on is a position nobody can trust.

THE PRICE IS SET ON THE OPEN LINE, not on twenty-two closed ones. Beside the field are the two figures that decide it -- what it cost and what you currently ask -- so the number is typed against them rather than from memory.

THE VERDICT COMES BEFORE THE TAP. Above: kept 8.5%, and what the lot raises. Below: 15,000 under cost, 120,000 across the eight, 760,000 back in the drawer -- named in shillings, never blocked, and ending "cash now against stock forever is your call, and this will not stop you making it." That is the existing screen's own copy and it is right.

SOMEBODY ELSE'S GOODS IS A DIFFERENT LOSS. Six of the eight barrows are a consignor's; you owe 104,000 each whatever they sell for, so 95,000 is 54,000 out of your own pocket. Amber, separate from the below-cost verdict, and it names how many of the eight it applies to -- the current screen treats the whole holding as consigned when any lot is.

THE OFFER IS ON THE LINE. Three buyers, most units first, ranked by what they have actually taken. One is open with the message written; the others are one tap. The buyer with no number on file is still LISTED, with "Copy" instead of "Send" and one line saying why -- named rather than dropped.

AND WHEN THERE IS NOBODY: the wheelbarrows have never been bought by anybody on the books -- both sales were counter sales with no name. So the line says that, and offers a shelf card instead of pretending a message is possible. That is the current screen's best paragraph, moved from the bottom of the page onto the line it is about.

THE THREE STATES A SCREEN IS ONLY DESIGNED ONCE YOU HAVE DRAWN >

NO STRIP OF ZEROS. Four tiles reading 0 fills a healthy screen with figures that mean nothing and makes a good shelf look like a broken app. The settled state carries three real figures instead -- including the thinnest line you sold, which is the one reading of "nothing to fix" worth anything: it tells you how close the bar came to catching something.

"NOTHING TO FIX" AND "NOTHING THAT CAN BE JUDGED" ARE DIFFERENT SCREENS. The first is good news. The second is 58 lines that sold with no cost behind them -- the app cannot say what they kept, and saying "everything is fine" would be a lie by omission. It names the number and offers the door that fixes it.

THE THIRD STATE DOES NOT EXIST TODAY. If the stock ledger fails to read, Clearance currently shows "Nothing is sitting still" -- a failed load and a clean shelf are indistinguishable, and only one of them is good news. The app's own law says a failure must name itself: so it says what failed, when the last good read was, that those figures are NOT current and are not shown, and it turns repricing off. A price lifted against figures nobody can see is a price set blind.

THE PHONE -- its own design, not the table reflowed

820px is a switch, so this is drawn from scratch at 390: 44px navy bar, 26px page name, 15px body, 14-16px row padding, 44px+ hit targets, no fake status bar and no fake keyboard.

THE PHONE JOB IS DIFFERENT FROM THE DESK JOB. At the desk you work down a ranked list deciding a day's prices. On a phone you are STANDING AT THE SHELF looking at something dusty, or a buyer is in front of you asking what you will take for the lot in the corner. So search comes first and asks "What are you holding?", and the card leads with the two figures that answer the question in front of you: what you charge now, and what you should.

TWO PRICES, NOT THREE. The desk shows cost, price, target price and the month it is worth. At 390px a third cell clips the figure it exists to show, so cost drops to the meta line -- it is a supporting fact, not the decision.

THE CARDS CARRY NO BUTTON. A "Charge" button on every card is fourteen oxide buttons on a screen allowed one. The accent lives once, in the docked navy bar in the thumb zone -- the pattern Follow-ups, Debtors and Creditors already ship -- and it names the single line most worth fixing, so the default action is right without reading the list.

ONE THING TO DECIDE: whether the phone should let you actually CHANGE a price, or only read and mark clearance. A lift moves both the shelf price and the bought-in price, and a mis-tap in a yard is a wrong price on your biggest seller. I have drawn "Open it" rather than "Charge 58,600" for that reason -- the confirmation happens on the opened line. Say the word and it becomes read-only, with the dock marking a clearance price instead.
